questions: Which food group is used for growth and repair?
Why can no single food be a balanced diet on its own?
segments.say: Start with the plate. A balanced diet covers all seven food groups: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water - each with its own job. Point at each group on your student notes as it appears.

questions: About how much energy does 10 g of fat release?
Why is fatty food called energy-dense?
segments.say: Now weigh food as fuel. Carbohydrate and protein release about 17 kJ per gram, but fat releases about 37 kJ per gram - more than double. That is why a small fatty snack can out-fuel a large starchy one. Now try the energy question on your worksheet.

questions: What does the stomach do to food?
Which organ comes immediately after the stomach?
segments.say: Follow one bite through the pipeline: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine. Each stop does one stage of the job - chewing and starch first, churning in the stomach, then the long small intestine.

questions: Could lipase digest protein instead? Why not?
segments.say: Meet the enzymes, one nutrient each. Amylase breaks down starch, protease breaks down protein and lipase breaks down fat. No enzyme can cover for another - specificity is the point.

questions: Why does a folded, villi-covered wall absorb more?
Where do the absorbed nutrients go next?
segments.say: End at the villi. The small intestine wall is covered in tiny fingers that multiply its surface, and digested nutrients pass through them into the blood. Check your student notes for how the pipeline and the enzymes lead here.

questions: What still happens to food after it leaves the stomach?
segments.say: A common mistake puts the finish line in the wrong organ. Check your student notes and finish the exit ticket, following the food all the way to the villi.
segments.watchFor: Digestion finishes in the stomach. Listen for students who end the pipeline at the stomach. Send them back to scene 3: Digestion does not end in the stomach: it continues in the small intestine, where most absorption happens.
